snippet.title: Forgotten Massacre of Jacobite Rebellion Uncovered: Scotland's Darkest Secret
snippet.description:
Dan Snow explores a fascinating archaeological dig, revealing events of the 1692 Glencoe Massacre.

Join historian Dan Snow as he journeys to Glencoe in the Scottish Highlands to examine an astonishing new archaeological discovery: a hoard of coins likely hidden during one of the most shocking episodes in British history - the Glencoe Massacre. 

At 5am on 13th February 1692, 38 members of the Clan MacDonald were brutally murdered by Scottish government troops. Many of those that managed to flee over the mountains also perished in the freezing conditions. This event was especially horrifying because the MacDonalds of Glencoe had played host to their assailants for nearly two weeks before the surprise attack. It was an assault on their Highland hospitality. 

Dan meets archaeologists from the University of Glasgow and National Trust for Scotland, who are currently excavating the remains of settlements in Glencoe, to try to understand what life was like here for the MacDonalds and why this massacre took place. Was it a revenge attack instigated by clan rivalry? Or, with a new monarch on the throne of England and Scotland, King William III, were there greater forces at play?  The discovery of a hidden hoard of coins speaks volumes about the Macdonalds' response to their attackers' presence in Glencoe. 

If you want to find out even more about this tragic event, listen to Dan Snow's History Hit podcast 'The Glencoe Massacre'  (ad free for all our subscribers): https://podfollow.com/dan-snows-history-hit/

The University of Glasgow has a very useful website with information about the excavations in Glencoe: https://www.gla.ac.uk/news/headline_1127146_en.html

snippet.title: Archaeologists Found a Mountain That Wasn't Natural
snippet.description:
High atop a remote mountain stands one of the world's most extraordinary ancient monuments. Massive stone heads, towering statues, and a mysterious man-made summit have puzzled archaeologists for centuries. Built over 2,000 years ago, Nemrut Dag was designed to guard a royal tomb, yet despite decades of excavations and modern technology, the burial chamber has never been found. In this documentary, we explore the incredible engineering behind the monument, the purpose of its colossal statues, the secrets hidden beneath the mountain, and why one of archaeology's greatest mysteries remains unsolved.

snippet.description:
►FIND OUT MORE about my exploratory trip here:
https://adeptexpeditions.com/tours/italy-sardinia-miano/

Across the island of Sardinia, more than 7,000 massive stone towers still stand, built during the Bronze Age by a society that left no written history, no kings, and no palaces.

These structures, known as nuraghi, dominate the landscape of ancient Europe. But why were so many built? What role did they play in daily life, power, and belief? And how did a non-literate society create one of the densest monumental landscapes in prehistoric Europe?

In this episode of Ancient Mysteries, we explore the Nuragic civilization: its architecture, villages, sacred spaces, ritual practices, and the enduring legacy of its stone towers. This isn’t a story of a “lost” civilization, but of one that transformed an entire island and still resists simple explanations.

If this story makes you want to experience these sites firsthand, I’ll be exploring Nuragic Sardinia in person on an upcoming Italy and Sardinia antiquity tour.

snippet.title: How Iranians Lived Before Islam  — Why Was This Erased?
snippet.description:
How Iranians actually lived before Islam is a story so powerful that entire generations were never allowed to hear it — and when you see what ancient Persia truly looked like, you'll question everything you were taught about this region.

Long before the modern borders of the Middle East existed, Persia was running a civilization that the rest of the world couldn't touch. We're talking about the first empire in recorded history to declare human rights. A society where multiple religions existed side by side without slaughter. Women owned property, held royal titles, and commanded military units while most of the ancient world treated them as invisible. 

The Persians built underground irrigation systems still functioning thousands of years later, road networks that connected continents, and a postal service faster than anything Europe would create for another two millennia. 

Zoroastrianism shaped concepts of heaven, hell, and judgment day that later appeared in every major Western religion — but almost nobody connects those dots today. This video reconstructs daily life inside ancient Iran — from what ordinary families ate and wore to how the courts operated, how education worked, and what celebrations looked like before everything changed. 

The architecture alone at Persepolis tells a story most historians skim past on purpose. Every empire falls — but understanding what Persia built and how it lived before that fall is one of the most important untold stories in human history. Don't skip to the end. snippet.title: Before Machines there was this Ancient Tool
snippet.description:
A Maya metate and mano used for grinding cacao, dating to 500–300 BC during the Preclassic period.

Carved from stone in either Chiapas, Mexico or the highlands of Guatemala, this grinding set would have been used to crush cacao beans into a paste for one of the earliest forms of chocolate consumed in Mesoamerica over 2,300 years ago.

The flat stone is the metate, while the hand-held grinding stone is known as the mano. Beyond cacao, these tools were also used to grind maize, seeds and pigments, forming an essential part of daily life in ancient Maya society.

Chocolate held deep ritual and social importance among the Maya long before European contact, consumed as a bitter ceremonial drink often mixed with spices, flowers or maize.

snippet.title: It survived 3,400 years inside an Egyptian tomb
snippet.description:
Merit’s wig is a remarkably well-preserved human-hair wig from the 18th Dynasty of the New Kingdom (about 1425–1353 BC). It was found in 1906 in the intact tomb of Kha and Merit (TT8) at Deir el-Medina, and it is now in the Museo Egizio in Turin.

What makes it especially interesting is how much it reveals about ancient Egyptian grooming and fashion. The hair was sewn into a mesh base, parted at the center, styled into curls and ringlets, and finished with braids at the sides and back. It was stored inside a tall acacia-wood shrine-shaped wig box inscribed with Merit’s name, which helped preserve it so well
